lessons.title: Lambdas, Streams, Threads, and Concurrency
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Functional and Concurrent Programming

## Lambdas and Streams
Lambdas provide a clear and concise way to represent one-method interfaces using an expression. The Stream API lets you process collections declaratively.

```java
List<Integer> nums = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5);
int sum = nums.stream()
              .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0)
              .mapToInt(Integer::intValue)
              .sum(); // 6
```

## Threads and Concurrency
Threads allow parallel execution. You can create custom threads or use `ExecutorService`. Virtual Threads (Java 21) are lightweight threads that dramatically reduce the effort of writing high-throughput concurrent apps.
To prevent data corruption in shared memory, use `synchronized`, `Atomics`, or `ReentrantLock`.

**Common Mistakes:** 
- Modifying a stateful variable inside a Stream lambda (streams should be stateless/pure).
- Forgetting to `shutdown()` an ExecutorService.

**Recap:** You've learned to write functional data pipelines and manage parallel execution.

exercises.title: Stream Terminals
exercises.instructionMarkdown: In the Stream API, what is the difference between `map` and `collect`?
choices: `map` is an intermediate operation; `collect` is a terminal operation.

exercises.title: Filter and Sum
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Write a function `sumOfSquares` that takes an `int[]`. Return the sum of the squares of all elements that are strictly greater than 3.
hints: Loop through the array or use `Arrays.stream(nums)`.

exercises.title: Debug: Starting a Thread
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Fix the code to actually start the thread concurrently instead of just calling its run method synchronously.
hints: Calling `run()` directly runs the code on the main thread.
Use `start()` to spawn a new execution thread.
